Max, threshold and resting heart rate, and your zones

PacingLab estimates your maximum heart rate from hard workouts, the highest heart rate you held for 10 seconds, once two of them come close. Until then, or if you know your maximum from a test, enter it here. Each change is kept with the date it applies from, so older sessions are analysed with the values that held at the time.

The heart rate values that zones and training load are anchored on. Any value you enter wins; every value you leave empty PacingLab finds in your own data.

# Maximum heart rate
The highest heart rate you held for 10 seconds in a workout, once a second workout comes within 3 bpm of it. A lower bound: a maximal test can only show a higher value.

# Threshold heart rate
After Joe Friel's field test: in 30 minutes of running at the hardest pace you can hold, the average heart rate of the last 20 minutes. PacingLab looks for the hardest continuous half hour of running in the last year, without walking breaks and averaging at least 85 % of your maximum. Without one, 90 % of your maximum stands in.
- Runs that were not all-out give a value at or below your true threshold.
- Heat and long runs raise heart rate at the same effort, which can push it a few beats too high.

# Resting heart rate
The median of the values your watch measured during sleep over the last 30 nights.
Joe Friel\'s running zones, as a share of threshold heart rate.
Polarised model: the first ventilatory threshold (VT1) is placed at 90 % of threshold heart rate, the second (VT2) at threshold heart rate.

Which measures it shows, and in what order

A small widget shows the first figures of this list; a larger one shows more, and a 7-day chart of the first figure when there is room. Training status and vitals go on a line underneath. Drag a measure by its handle to move it; the eye hides it.
Days without work or a fixed start. Sleep timing compares the nights before them with the other nights.
How far above your usual week of running a week counts as above tolerance. More injuries came above 30 % in one study (Nielsen 2014); 10 % is a stricter rule of thumb without such evidence.
VO2max and aerobic efficiency of warm runs are raised by the cost of heat (Mantzios 2022). Decoupling only marks warm runs either way.
